Our Ethos
Kensington Wade is a school of opportunities: a place where children are challenged to become their best, to discover new talents and interests and to develop a global outlook, within a safe and nurturing community. It is also an award-winning English and Chinese international school in London, taking the best of British and Chinese culture and coupling this with academic excellence.
We value kindness, respect, integrity, intellectual curiosity and endeavour. We actively promote fundamental British values which underpin everything that we do.
Our Aims
We aim to provide an environment where pupils develop:
A love of learning
A spirit of curiosity and independent thought
Emotional and intellectual resilience

Head’s Welcome
Kensington Wade is an award-winning, immersive bilingual nursery and prep school which takes the best of British and Chinese culture and couples this with academic excellence.
Our child-centred approach, focussed on ensuring every individual boy and girl is challenged in all areas of their development, creates a happy, inspiring environment where all pupils thrive. Outstanding academic achievement and our exceptional preparation for 11+ assessments ensure our pupils progress to top senior schools.
At Kensington Wade, the immersive nature of the school means that lessons are taught in English and in Mandarin, giving children complete fluency in both languages. Although many children will join us with just one language they will leave us with at least two.
Our academic results are consistently outstanding and testament to the quality and excellence of our dual language provision. We offer specialist teaching from the very start with all children enjoying music lessons and, as they travel up the school, science, computing, Spanish, swimming and sports.
We also provide an extensive co-curricular programme with activities designed to challenge children intellectually, physically and creatively.
The happiness of our pupils is of paramount importance. We work closely with all our families to make sure that their children feel safe, valued and loved by every member of our staff.
I am thrilled to be Headmaster of what I consider to be the most exciting school in London. Please come and visit to discover what we have to offer.
ISI School Inspection Report 2025

Partnerships and outreach
At Kensington Wade we are committed to pursuing our aim to foster linguistic and cultural fluency beyond our own school gates into the community at large.
Working with local schools in our home borough of Hammersmith and Fulham, we are developing a comprehensive outreach programme offering a range of resources and opportunities.
Kensington Wade currently works with Melcombe Primary School in delivering Chinese language and culture lessons to older year groups, piloting the development of further lesson content. We plan to provide a full-year video content and lesson plan programme based around the Chinese calendar, and including introductory material on the Chinese language, for schools to integrate into their cultural curriculum.
We are working to broaden these opportunities to include cultural exchanges and partnerships with bilingual schools in China and the United States, cultural visits to schools, online programmes and summer camp events. We plan to extend our free resources offering to schools across London and the UK.
Kensington Wade also partners with schools internationally, including joint events and pen pal schemes, and we encourage our pupils to be active members of our local community through visits and performances.
For further information or to make a connection with us, please email office@kensingtonwade.com and you will be directed to the appropriate member of the leadership team.
ISI School Inspection Report 2025

pageCache.pageTitle: Kensington Wade | Five Questions to Ask on a School Open DayFive Questions to Ask on a School Open Day
pageCache.text:
Five Questions to Ask on a School Open Day
Open days are carefully choreographed. The school knows which rooms look their best, which teachers give the warmest welcome, and which pupils are most likely to make a good impression. None of this is deceptive. It reflects genuine pride in what the school offers.
But you are not there to be impressed by what the school wants you to see. You are there to find out what you need to know to make a good decision for your child. These five questions are designed to help you do exactly that.
1. What Happens When a Child Is Struggling?
This is the single most revealing question you can ask on a school visit, and most parents don’t think to ask it. Schools are practised at describing how they support high-attaining pupils. Fewer have a genuinely well-developed answer for what they do when a child finds things hard. Listen for specifics: who identifies the difficulty, how quickly, and what happens next? The quality of the answer will tell you a great deal about the school’s real values.
At Kensington Wade, we would tell you that our teachers know their pupils individually, that we assess regularly and adjust our approach quickly, and that parents are brought into the conversation early rather than late. We believe transparency about difficulty is part of genuine partnership with families.
2. How Are the Most Able Pupils Challenged?
What does extension look like in a typical lesson, rather than just in after-school clubs? Are the most able pupils given more of the same, or genuinely different and more demanding work? Ask to see an example of a Year 5 or 6 project. The standard of independent work at the top of the school is a good proxy for the ambition of the curriculum overall. Our Prep School page gives a detailed overview of how curriculum challenge is structured at Kensington Wade.
3. What Does a Typical Day Actually Look Like?
What you want to understand is the texture of daily life: how the timetable works, what transitions between lessons feel like, what children do at lunchtime, how much of the day is teacher-led versus pupil-led. Ask a teacher or pupil guide to walk you through a typical Tuesday. You will learn more from that than from any amount of aspirational language about breadth and balance.
4. How Do You Communicate With Parents?
Communication style is a surprisingly accurate indicator of school culture. Schools that communicate proactively, with context and honesty, rather than reactively and only when something has gone wrong, view parents as genuine partners. Ask specifically about how the school communicates progress throughout the year, not just at formal reporting points. Ask how easy it is to speak to a class teacher, and how quickly messages are typically responded to.
5. Where Do Your Leavers Go, and Why?
For a prep school, this question reveals whether the school takes a thoughtful, individualised approach to senior school placement, or effectively channels pupils towards a small number of preferred schools regardless of fit. A good answer describes the range of schools pupils go to, acknowledges that the right senior school depends on the child, and gives a sense of how the school prepares pupils for interviews and entrance assessments.
At Kensington Wade, our leavers go to a wide range of competitive senior schools. We prepare them not just academically but in terms of the confidence, cultural awareness and self-possession that make those processes go well.
One More Thing: Bring Your Child
If at all possible, bring your child to the open day, or arrange a separate taster visit. Children respond to environments in ways that are immediate and honest. Watch whether your child leans in or draws back, and whether they talk about it on the way home. Their instincts are worth listening to.
We offer individual family visits and taster sessions at Kensington Wade so prospective families can see the school in a relaxed, personalised way. Book a place or get in touch on our Visit the School page.
ISI School Inspection Report 2025

pageCache.text:
Our Founders
Adrian Richardson
Adrian Richardson was educated aboard the Training Ship Mercury, one of the 30 pre-sea training schools founded in the late 19th century to meet the needs of Britain’s Royal and merchant navies. The ship itself was a converted barque that served as a school dormitory with boys rowing to and from lessons on the mainland each day. Richardson left Mercury in 1959 with the intention of joining the Royal Navy. Unfortunately, Naval College revealed him to be slightly colourblind so he had to settle for a stint working at British India, then part of the PNO group. He travelled widely in Australia and South Asia.
In September 1961, when on leave, staying with his parents, Richardson saw advertisement for a junior teaching position at Oxfordshire prep school called Cothill. He took a job as a junior geography master, which job began a relationship with Cothill of more than 50 happy years. By 1976 Richardson was the headmaster and there followed many years of expansion and improvement. In 1990 Richardson bought and opened as a bilingual French English school, the Château de Sauveterre, 50 miles south of Toulouse. In 1993 he purchased Chandlings Manor.
By 2003 Richardson had been promoted from headmaster to principal of the trust he created, the Cothill Educational Trust. In 2007 the trust bought Martin Hall and Kitebrook House. In 2008 he set up the Old Mouse Tree School and in 2009 bought Ashdown house. Later saw the acquisition of St Albans school and Barfield school.
Richardson joined Hugo de Burgh in 2015 with the intention that he be the (honorary) CEO of the Anglo Chinese School of London, as was the first name of Kensington Wade. Together they spent two years travelling all over London trying to find buildings and making presentations to potential backers. Eventually, thanks to Toby Young and Lord Nash, then Schools Minister, they obtained a lease on the new school building intended for West London preschools, in 2016. Chinese friends and the founders put up the initial capital.
Adrian Richardson was already ill at the launch of Kensington Wade by Lord Willetts and Lord Nash in 2017. He attended and was thrilled to see that his dreams for Europe’s first bilingual Chinese English school were coming true. Greatly missed by the staff, parents and founders of KW, as by so many people connected with Cothill, he passed away soon after. His wife, Rachel Richardson, joined the board of governors, soon after.
Dr Zeng Rong 曾荣
Dr Zeng Rong graduated from Peking University and the London School of Economics, before taking her PhD at the University of Westminster on the effects of globalization on UK and Chinese screen media.
She then helped the set up the China Media Centre at the University of Westminster (now CUKCI at Goldsmiths, University of London) and worked as its China representative for over 10 years. She has brought Chinese television personnel in large numbers to the UK to study and develop ideas with experienced British programme development executives and producers, who have gained contracts and commissions in China as a result.
She established Houghton Street Media (HSM) in 2013 in Beijing, making screen media with social purpose, particularly linked to healthcare, childrearing and conditions such as Alzheimer. HSM has produced many top TV shows and won hundreds of awards in the last 10 years. She executive produced China Treading Now, Beloved Life, BLK946, Forget Me Not Café (season 1-3), Stories in Accident and Emergency (season 1-2), Life Unlimited (1-2), Come on Baby, We are Teenagers, Gadget Show China, The West You Really Don’t Know, etc.
Prof Hugo de Burgh 戴雨果教授
Hugo de Burgh is Director of China UK Creative Industries @Goldsmiths College, University of London. He started working life as a community development worker in impoverished areas of Scotland. Activism led him into broadcast journalism, focussing on poverty, undereducation and employability, and then to teaching journalism in Nottingham, in London and in China. He recently completed a fourth term at Tsinghua University, as Walt Disney Professor of Media and Communications in Schwarzman, the US college of international relations.
Hugo de Burgh has initiated and run, in collaboration with many others, a further education college (Castlecliff Training Centre, Edinburgh), a TV production company making social issue actuality for STV, BBC and C4 (DBF Communications) and London’s China Media Centre, connecting the creative industries of UK and China and now housed in Goldsmiths College. He has authored or co-authored 15 books. His China’s Media in the Emerging World Order (2020) describes and analyses a burgeoning global power of the 21st century. Investigative Journalism (2021) tracks the emergence of new tools and techniques for holding power to account and maps emerging models of global cross -border collaboration and exposure. Earlier books have dealt with environment reporting, how China works and the functions of journalists in the globalised, digitised, world.
His first novel, TO THE RIVER, why would you risk your life, and all that you love, for a stranger? was launched at the Mansion House by Lord Mayor Michael Mainelli in September 2024. It is a reflection on altruism, set in warn-torn Italy, 1943. A new interpretation of the four British nations, WHO ARE WE, and how will we survive in the Age of Asia? (Cambridge: CamRivers) was launched by Sir Vince Cable at the London School of Economics in November 2024.
ISI School Inspection Report 2025

pageCache.text:
Curriculum
Kensington Wade follows the British curriculum except in mathematics where we follow the Shanghai Approach (also called the Mastery Approach). The unique advantage at Kensington Wade is that we teach the curriculum in a fully immersive bilingual setting.
Reception
Pupils in Reception at Kensington Wade continue to follow the Early Years Foundation Framework covering the seven areas of learning:
Communication and language
Physical development
Personal, social and emotional development
Literacy
Mathematics
Understanding the world
Expressive arts and design
Year 1
Entering Key Stage 1, pupils in Year 1 experience a more formal style of learning with carpet instruction and follow-up learning at their tables. Children follow the Shanghai Approach in mathematics (also called the Maths Mastery approach) and through this the children securely underpin their conceptual understanding in mathematics through concrete, pictorial and abstract forms.
In English, pupils develop their reading and comprehension skills, writing and spelling and spoken language proficiency with daily phonics to scaffold this. Daily Chinese literacy lessons develop pupils’ understanding of spoken Chinese as well as introducing them to reading and writing the Chinese characters.
Children also benefit from immersive lessons such as art, humanities and science, delivered in either English or Chinese. In addition, they have specialist teachers in music and sport and take part in swimming lessons which are provided locally.
Children take part in termly class assemblies and performances, in both English and Chinese, ensuring they move on to Year 2 with confidence and enthusiasm for performance.
Year 2
Year 2 is the second year of Key Stage 1. The children are developing as independent learners and continue the Maths Mastery approach following Power Maths and daily English and Chinese lessons as they did in Year 1.
Pupils continue to benefit from the opportunities of specialist teaching in music with a weekly choir session in addition to their music provision. Children can also start individual music lessons in piano and violin in our dedicated music room or 1:1 room. They continue with specialist sport lessons twice a week.
Year 3
Entering Key Stage 2, pupils in Year 3 experience a step up in excitement and challenge. They continue with the Maths Mastery curriculum, daily English and Chinese lessons and immersive lessons in humanities and PSHE delivered in either English or Chinese.
The children benefit from continued specialist teaching in music and sport and start to receive teaching from our subject specialists in art, computing and science. They continue their swimming lessons and begin to represent the school in team sports fixtures and competitions such as the ISA STEAM events. From Year 3 the curriculum also includes debating and reasoning and children take part in their first ESB speech and language exams.
A notable highlight for pupils in Year 3 is their first residential visit. Most recently, pupils took part in a three day trip to Hooke Court in Dorset where they explored a range of activities including mapping and orienteering, archaeology and environmental science.
Starting Key Stage 2 marks the start of our 11+ preparations and we take a calm and measured approach to support our pupils on this journey.
Year 4
Pupils continue to develop as independent learners in Year 4 and have the same balance of immersive English and Chinese and curriculum subjects as in Year 3.
In Year 4 we see the introduction of a Reading Challenge Competition which gives the children vital practice in speaking aloud and maintaining the interest of their audience. By this point the children will be mastering, if not already mastered, their brilliant penmanship and are rewarded with a pen licence allowing them to complete their daily work in pen rather than pencil.
Children are encouraged to become more responsible for their own belongings and to organise their time, for example, in prioritising homework and meeting deadlines.
Year 5
Pupils continue to develop as independent learners in Year 5 and have the same balance of immersive English and Chinese and curriculum subjects as in Year 4 with the addition of Spanish which is delivered by a specialist native-speaking teacher.
The children in Year 5 have the opportunity to go further afield for their residential trip. This year our Year 5 pupils will be staying at a residential centre on the Isle of Wight to take part in team building activities over three days.
Year 6
By the end of Key Stage 2 pupils are fully prepared for the 11+ process and we focus on supporting them both academically and pastorally, with a balance towards the English immersive classroom as they carry out these English exams. Close and regular communication between school and home ensures this is a well-managed and smooth process.
Pupils continue with their lessons in the spring and summer terms to ensure they are fully prepared for their transition to Year 7 in their chosen senior school. In addition, we intend to put all our pupils’ hard work in becoming fluent in Chinese into practice with an extended residential trip to mainland China.
Children also take on leadership roles in this final year as House and Subject Leaders.
ISI School Inspection Report 2025

pageCache.pageTitle: Kensington Wade | GCSE’s at age 11 for Kensington Wade pupils - Kensington WadeGCSE’s at age 11 for Kensington Wade pupils - Kensington Wade
pageCache.text:
GCSE’s at age 11 for Kensington Wade pupils
Six of our students have taken their GCSE five years early and achieved exceptional results. The students, many of whom had no Chinese background prior to joining us, have taken their Mandarin GCSE in Year 6.
Huw May, Head of Kensington Wade, commented: “The gifts of a bilingual education are so clear to see. The bilingual brain increases the mental flexibility of the pupils and the ability to switch between tasks, coupled with superb problem-solving skills, gives them an academic advantage.
We empower happy children to be at their best and take on the exciting challenges of life. Being able to take a GCSE at such a young age is a great example of this”
As demand for Mandarin continues to grow across the UK, Kensington Wade remains at the forefront of bilingual education, offering a unique and future-focused learning experience.
Results also featured in the FulhamSW6 write up.

A Parent’s Guide to Mid-Autumn Festival: Traditions, Mooncakes and Meaning
Every autumn, when the harvest moon climbs to its fullest and brightest, families across the Chinese-speaking world gather to share mooncakes, light lanterns and gaze at the sky together. Mid-Autumn Festival, known as Zhongqiu Jie, is one of the most important celebrations in the Chinese cultural calendar, and at Kensington Wade it is one of the most anticipated dates in our school year.
If you’re new to the festival, this guide covers where it comes from, what the key traditions mean, and how your family can enjoy a little of it at home.
Where Does Mid-Autumn Festival Come From?
Mid-Autumn Festival falls on the 15th day of the eighth month in the Chinese lunar calendar, the night when the moon is believed to be at its most perfectly round. That roundness is no coincidence: in Chinese culture, a full circle symbolises completeness and reunion, making this a festival above all about family togetherness.
The festival’s origins are thousands of years old, tied to harvest thanksgiving and moon worship. The most beloved story associated with it is that of Chang’e, the Moon Goddess, who drank an elixir of immortality and floated up to the moon to live there forever, watched over by the Jade Rabbit who pounds medicine in a mortar. Our pupils encounter these stories through Mandarin lessons, cultural studies and the school’s own celebrations.
The Key Traditions Explained
Mooncakes are the festival’s most iconic symbol. These dense, round pastries, typically filled with lotus seed paste or red bean and often with a salted egg yolk at the centre representing the moon, are gifted between families and shared after dinner. A beginner-friendly recipe is included below.
Lanterns, traditionally paper and now often LED, are carried by children in the evening. At Kensington Wade, pupils make their own lanterns in art lessons in the lead-up to the celebration. The warm glow of dozens of lanterns held aloft is one of those sights that stays with children long into adulthood.
Moon gazing is perhaps the simplest tradition, and the one easiest to share at home. On the night of the festival, step outside with your child, look up together, and ask them what they see. In Chinese folklore, they might spot the silhouette of Chang’e or the Jade Rabbit.
How Kensington Wade Celebrates
Our Mid-Autumn Festival celebration weaves together music, storytelling, art and food in a way that makes the cultural learning vivid and memorable. Pupils learn the story of Chang’e in Mandarin, practise festival vocabulary, and take part in lantern-making workshops. This kind of lived cultural experience sits at the heart of school life at Kensington Wade, where Chinese culture is not a topic covered in a single lesson but something woven through the whole school year.
Try It at Home: A Simple Mooncake Activity
You don’t need to be an expert baker to bring this tradition home. Here is a simple no-bake version suitable for primary-age children:
Make the activity richer by asking your child to tell you the story of Chang’e while you cook together.
Come and See the School in Action
Mid-Autumn Festival is one of many celebrations that bring the Kensington Wade community together throughout the year. If you’d like to experience that community for yourself, you’re very welcome to join us at one of our open events. You can book a place or arrange a personal tour on our Visit the School page.

Music
What is the role of music at Kensington Wade?
Music is an important part of life at Kensington Wade. The children in every year group, from Nursery to Year 6, have at least two music lessons per week from a specialist teacher, during which they are exposed to a variety of musical opportunities through singing, listening, composing and performing.
This consistent exposure helps to build confidence, creativity and a lifelong appreciation of music. Music also plays a key role in supporting wider learning, enhancing memory, coordination and emotional expression.
How is Chinese music integrated into learning?
Pupils also immerse themselves in Chinese music, one of the world’s oldest and most complex musical systems. They learn the Hulusi (葫芦丝) alongside the recorder, perform on Chinese percussion instruments, learn Peking Opera performance skills and study Jianpu (简谱) notation.
This unique aspect of the curriculum deepens pupils’ cultural understanding and enriches their bilingual experience. It also allows children to engage with music in a way that reflects the school’s bicultural ethos.
What additional music opportunities are available?
In addition to classroom music, we offer in-school instrumental lessons and an extensive range of optional music extension including:
These opportunities enable pupils to develop their individual talents and pursue their musical interests in greater depth. Many children choose to participate in multiple activities, further enhancing their skills and enjoyment.
Choirs and orchestra
Chinese music club
Musical theatre
Composition and music technology club
How do pupils perform and showcase their work?
Children are encouraged to celebrate their hard work and achievements throughout the year with a wide range of performance opportunities. These include Christmas nativity plays, termly assemblies and instrumental concerts and an end of year Chinese production.
Regular performance opportunities help to build confidence and stage presence, while also fostering a strong sense of community. They provide pupils with memorable experiences and the chance to share their progress with families and friends.

Learning
At Kensington Wade, our nursery is the stepping stone to school, where pupils learn within a stimulating environment which encourages them to work and play in a variety of ways. Our teachers give children the opportunity to investigate and build on their interests and extend their knowledge and skills.
Nursery classes at Kensington Wade follow the Early Years Foundation Framework covering the seven areas of learning:
The curriculum at Kensington Wade is delivered through our immersive bilingual model which allows children to be exposed to both languages for equal amounts of time. This environment imitates how children learned their first language: new vocabulary is introduced in an everyday context and within a secure, engaging and supportive community. Children in nursery also receive sport and music lessons from specialist teachers.

What Is The Learning Environment In The Nursery?
The nursery offers a fully immersive bilingual environment, blending English and Chinese across a rich curriculum in a nurturing and stimulating setting.
1. Immersive Bilingual Setting
Children spend equal time in English and Chinese learning environments, with each lesson delivered in one language at a time.
2. Comprehensive Curriculum
Nursery covers Communication, Language & Literacy (CLL) in both languages, Phonics, Maths, PSED, Music, Sport, plus the full EYFS framework.
3. Stimulating Indoor and Outdoor Spaces
The nursery is situated in a standalone, open-plan building with both indoor and outdoor areas that encourage self-directed play, such as cooking, painting, and water play.
4. Experienced and Caring Staff
A full complement of teachers and assistants ensures high levels of direct contact, stimulation, and encouragement for every child.
5. Preparation for Continuous Progress
The nursery builds strong foundations in both languages and developmental areas, setting children up smoothly for Reception and beyond.

Wellbeing & Pastoral Care
How does Kensington Wade support the wellbeing and pastoral care of its pupils?
The happiness and wellbeing of our children is a huge priority at Kensington Wade and we have an open and caring culture. We work extremely closely with our families to make sure that their children feel safe and loved by every member of our staff.
This strong sense of care underpins every aspect of school life and ensures that pupils feel confident, secure and ready to learn.
How are pupils supported as individuals?
Every pupil at Kensington Wade is genuinely known as an individual by all staff and every child is treated as an important member of our school community. Every child has an individual learning plan that is updated and shared with the Headmaster every week.
We value the opinions of our pupils and they have the opportunity to represent our School Council and Eco Club. We actively offer opportunities for every child to succeed and we all celebrate and share their happiness when they do.
This personalised approach helps to build confidence, resilience and a strong sense of belonging within the school.
How is wellbeing monitored and communicated?
We have dedicated time at staff meetings for pastoral care matters and the Head meets regularly with teaching staff to discuss pupils’ wellbeing and progress.
Form teachers hold termly progress meetings with their parents and, as a school, Kensington Wade has an ‘open door’ policy with parents encouraged to come into school to share any concerns they may have with us.
This regular communication ensures that any concerns are addressed quickly and that every child is fully supported.
How does the school work with families?
At Kensington Wade we foster close relationships with our families, and we are most definitely a school for all children.
It does not matter if a child’s family does not speak Chinese, we are well equipped for this and provide support for help at home.
We are committed to working in partnership with parents, offering guidance and reassurance so that every family feels included and supported as part of the school community.
ISI School Inspection Report 2025
